track-utm-campaigns:
A UTM campaign is a link you tag so you can tell one visit from another when the referrer is missing or useless. Email apps, mobile apps, and many social apps strip the referrer. Without tags, those visits land in "direct" and you cannot tell a newsletter from a stranger typing the URL. The tags are five query parameters. The hard part is naming them the same way every time, so the report does not split one campaign into six rows.

The five parameters

Only the first three are required for a useful report. The last two are optional and worth using when you are testing more than one creative.

  • utm_source is where the click came from: newsletter, google, linkedin, partner-site.
  • utm_medium is the channel type: email, cpc, social, referral.
  • utm_campaign is the effort: november-launch, docs-refresh, black-friday. One name per effort, reused across sources.
  • utm_term is the paid keyword, when you have one. Skip it on email and organic social.
  • utm_content tells creatives apart: hero, footer, text-link.

A link you can read out loud

This is a newsletter link to a pricing page. Source, medium, campaign, and which button:

https://example.com/pricing?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=november-launch&utm_content=hero

Build that URL in the UTM campaign URL builder. It runs in the browser and does not upload the address. Pick a preset (Google, email, LinkedIn, and the others on that page) when you want a conventional medium, then edit the campaign name. Copy the result into the email tool or the ad.

Naming rules that keep the report to one row

Analytics tools treat Newsletter, newsletter, and news_letter as three sources. Pick one spelling and write it down. These rules are enough for a small site:

  • Lowercase only. Hyphens, not spaces or underscores.
  • One canonical source per place. The Sunday email is always newsletter, never mailchimp one week and email the next. Put the tool name in the campaign if you need it (november-launch), not in the source.
  • Medium is the channel, not the tool. email, cpc, social, referral. Pulzivo groups cpc, ppc, and paid as Paid Search, email as Email, and social as Social Media. If you invent utm_medium=newsletter, you lose that grouping and the row sits on its own.
  • Campaign names stay stable for the life of the effort. Do not append the send date to the campaign if you want the three sends added together. Put the date in utm_content (nov-21) when you need to split them.
  • Do not tag links inside your own site. An internal link with UTMs overwrites the campaign that actually brought the visitor. Tag the link that leaves the other site, the ad, or the email, and stop there.

Write a one-page cheat sheet

Before the next launch, list the sources you really use. A typical indie list is short: newsletter / email, google / cpc, linkedin / social, docs-partner / referral. Share that list with anyone who sends a link, including yourself in two months. The builder presets cover the common pairs. The cheat sheet covers the campaign names, which are yours.

What shows up in Pulzivo

The script reads utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_term, and utm_content when it loads, including on the first page of a visit. That matters on a React, Angular, or Next.js app, because the router sometimes strips the query during boot. The landing snapshot is taken before that happens. Installation is the same script tag as the rest of the product. The steps are in the documentation.

On the dashboard, UTM and attribution reports are part of Starter and above, not the free plan. The free plan is still 10,000 events a month and records page views, clicks, custom events, scroll depth, and Web Vitals, so you can install now and read campaign rows after you move to Starter. You can also turn UTM capture off for a site with setPreferences({ utm_attribution: false }) if you have a reason to drop the parameters. Plan limits and the Starter feature list are on the pricing page.

Check one real click before the campaign goes out

Send the tagged URL to yourself, open it, and confirm the page view carries the five values you typed. Fix the spelling in the email tool, not in the report, if a source looks wrong. A report cannot merge linked-in and linkedin after the fact without an export and a spreadsheet.

Keep a note of the campaign names you have already used. Reusing november-launch on the next email adds to the same row, which is what you want when it is still that launch. Starting a fresh name, november-launch-2, splits the history. Decide that before the second send, not after you have two half-rows.

What UTMs will not do

They do not identify a person. They describe the link. They do not survive if the visitor copies the address bar and deletes the query, and they do not repair a campaign that used a different name last month. They also do not replace a custom event. "Clicked the ad" is a UTM. "Finished signup" is PulzivoAnalytics('event', 'signup_completed', { plan: 'free' }), which is available on every plan, including Free.

Tag the next email with one consistent source, medium, and campaign. When you want those rows in the dashboard, Starter is the plan that includes them. Start free if you do not have an account yet, and use the builder for the URL so a missing parameter does not ship.
core-web-vitals-for-site-owners:
Core Web Vitals are three field measurements of how a page feels: how long until the main content appears, how quickly the page reacts to a tap or a click, and how much the layout jumps while it loads. Google publishes them, search tools surface them, and they are easy to misread if you only have a lab score from your own laptop. This is the owner’s version: what each number means, which cutoffs are "good", and how to get the numbers from real visits.

The three numbers

LCP, largest contentful paint

LCP is the time until the largest visible piece of content is painted. On a marketing page that is usually the hero image or the main headline block. On a docs page it is often the title plus the first paragraph. Google's published guidance treats 2.5 seconds or less as good and more than 4.0 seconds as poor. Between those, the rating is "needs improvement". Pulzivo uses those same cutoffs.

A slow LCP is usually one of a short list: a hero image that is larger than the slot it sits in, a font that blocks the first paint, a server that is slow to send HTML, or a script in the head that runs before the content. You do not need a performance project to test the first one. Serve a reasonably sized image, give it width and height, and load it early.

INP, interaction to next paint

INP measures how long the page takes to show the next frame after a visitor clicks, taps, or presses a key. It replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital. Good is 200 milliseconds or less. Poor is more than 500 milliseconds. The number people feel is the worst of the interactions on that page, not the average of the easy ones.

A bad INP is almost always JavaScript. A click handler that sorts a large list, a third-party widget that locks the main thread, or a framework re-render of the whole page will push it over the line. The fix is to do less work on the interaction, not to buy a faster laptop. Lab tools on a developer machine often miss this, because the machine is idle and the page is warm.

CLS, cumulative layout shift

CLS measures unexpected movement of content. Good is 0.1 or less. Poor is more than 0.25. The classic causes are an image or an ad without reserved space, a banner injected above the article after load, and a web font that swaps and reflows the paragraph. A shift the visitor caused, such as opening an accordion, is not the problem you are hunting. The problem is the page moving while they are trying to read or tap.

Reserve the space. Put width and height on images, or use CSS aspect-ratio. Do not insert a cookie-style bar or a promo above the content after the first paint. If a late element has to appear, put it below the fold or over a placeholder of the same size.

Field data, not a single Lighthouse run

Lighthouse and PageSpeed Insights are useful lab checks. They load the page once, on one device profile, and tell you what might be slow. Core Web Vitals, as Google uses them for ranking reports, are field data: the experience of real visitors, typically looked at as a 75th percentile. One fast run on your office connection does not mean the 75th percentile visitor on a phone had a good LCP.

Pulzivo records LCP, INP, and CLS in the browser with a PerformanceObserver and sends them as Web Vital events. The dashboard rates the 75th percentile against the cutoffs above. Web Vitals are on the free plan, along with page views, clicks, custom events, and scroll depth. You do not need Starter or above to see them. The plan grid is on the pricing page, and the install is the same script tag described in the documentation.

How to read the card

  • Look at the 75th percentile, not the average. The average hides the slow quarter of visits.
  • Read it per page. A homepage with a giant image and a docs page full of text will not share an LCP.
  • Ignore a rating with a tiny sample. A handful of visits is not a distribution. Wait until the page has real traffic before you redesign around one red number.
  • Compare a page to itself over time. A deploy that adds a chat widget is easier to spot that way than a comparison against an unrelated site.

A practical order of fixes

If LCP is poor, start with the largest element. In the browser's performance panel, find which node was the LCP element, then shrink it or load it sooner. If INP is poor, record a click on the slow control with the performance panel and look for a long task. If CLS is poor, reload the page and watch what jumps. Those three checks solve more owner-facing problems than a generic "improve your score" pass.

Third-party scripts, including analytics, sit on the same thread. Pulzivo's core script is about 9KB gzip, which is small next to a tag manager full of pixels, but it is not free. If you are chasing INP, measure before and after you add any script. The features page lists what the free script records automatically, so you can see whether you still need the other tags.

What this will not tell you

Web Vitals do not say whether the copy is clear, whether the form is too long, or whether anyone finished signup. They say whether the page was slow, sluggish, or jumpy for real visits. Pair them with the page list and, when you have them, with scroll depth. A fast page that nobody scrolls is a content problem. A slow page that people still finish is a performance problem you can schedule.

Install the script, open a page you actually care about, and read LCP, INP, and CLS at the 75th percentile before you change the design. The free plan includes those metrics. Start free and give it a few days of real traffic before you treat a lab score as the answer.
what-cookieless-analytics-means:
"Cookieless analytics" has become a label. Vendors use it to mean different things, and a reader can easily walk away thinking it means "we store nothing" or "you never need to think about consent." Neither of those follows from the phrase. This page is the careful version: what the word actually describes, what it does not decide for you, and how Pulzivo implements it. It is not legal advice. Whether your site needs a banner depends on your jurisdiction and on everything else you load, not on a slogan.

What the word refers to

A cookie is a small name-value pair the browser stores and sends back to the site on later requests. Analytics products have used one, often for a year or two, as a client id so they can tell a returning browser from a new one. "Cookieless" means the analytics script does not set that kind of cookie. It does not mean the product has no identifier at all, and it does not mean the browser holds nothing.

Cookie, localStorage, and memory

localStorage is a different browser API. It is not sent automatically with every request the way a cookie is, and it does not expire on its own. A script can still keep a random id there. sessionStorage lasts for the tab. A value held only in memory disappears on refresh. A product can be cookieless and still use one or more of those. If a vendor says "cookieless," the useful follow-up is: what, if anything, do you write to the device, how long does it live, and does it identify a person?

Google's documentation describes GA4's JavaScript tags as using first-party cookies such as _ga. That is a cookie-based design, whatever else the product does. The comparison is on the Pulzivo vs Google Analytics page, including where GA4 remains the better fit.

What Pulzivo does

Pulzivo's script does not set an analytics cookie. By default it keeps an anonymous visitor id in localStorage, stamped with the calendar day. On a new day it mints a new id. Nothing in that value ties today's visits to yesterday's. A session id, also in localStorage, rolls over after a period of inactivity so one sitting is separate from the whole day. The mechanics, including Do Not Track, Global Privacy Control, and optOut(), are written up on the cookieless analytics page. This article is the definition. That page is the implementation.

No personal data is collected by default. The ordinary event is a page path, a title, a referrer, and the rotating id. An email is sent only if your code calls identify() or sets an email, and that path is opt-in. A permanent id (pz_uid) is written only after identify() on the Pro plan, using an id you supply. Until you do that, there is no stable visitor key.

What you can still measure

  • On the free plan: page views, clicks, custom events, scroll depth, and Core Web Vitals. The allowance is 10,000 events a month.
  • On Starter: sessions, unique visitors within the way the product defines them, and UTM attribution.
  • On Pro: opt-in identification and JavaScript errors.
  • On Enterprise: form abandonment, rage clicks, and dead clicks.

Daily rotation means the free product cannot, by itself, connect yesterday's anonymous reader to today's signup. If you need that, pass your own id on Pro. If you do not, you still have page, source, and action counts. The plan list is on the pricing page.

What the label does not decide

Cookieless is not a statement about the law. Some regions regulate localStorage and similar storage, not only cookies. A product that sets no cookie can still be something you need to describe in a privacy policy, and it can still sit next to other scripts on your page that do set cookies. Pulzivo does not promise that you can skip a banner. It promises not to set a cookie and not to collect personal data by default. The rest is a question for someone qualified to look at your site.

Cookieless is also not the same as "anonymous in every sense." The rotating id distinguishes browsers for a day so the dashboard is not a single total. IP addresses may be used in transit to derive a coarse location and then not stored as a personal profile. Read the vendor's actual policy. A marketing sentence is not the policy.

Questions worth asking any vendor

  • Does the script call the cookie API? If the answer is no, ask what it writes to localStorage or sessionStorage and when that value changes.
  • Is there a long-lived id by default, or only after you pass one?
  • Can a visitor turn collection off, and does the script honor Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control?
  • What do you do with an email if the customer sends one by accident inside an event property? Pulzivo redacts email-shaped strings. You should still not put an email in a custom property.

A plain description you can reuse

For a privacy page, a precise sentence beats a slogan: the analytics script sets no cookies and collects no personal data by default. It stores an anonymous id that changes each calendar day, plus a session id, in localStorage. A name, an email, or a stable id is sent only if the site opts in and supplies the value. Adjust that sentence if you have called identify(), because then you are sending an id you chose.

The core script is about 9KB gzip. That size is unrelated to the cookie question, but it is the script you are describing. If you want to see the default payload on your own site, start free. The free plan is 10,000 events a month, and you can read the cookieless page linked above before you turn any opt-in identity on.
rage-clicks-and-dead-clicks:
A rage click is a visitor hitting the same control over and over because nothing seemed to happen. A dead click is a click that does not navigate, does not scroll the page, and is not a click into a form field. Both are clues about the interface, not about the person's mood. Used carefully, they tell you which button, link, or card is wasting a visit. Used carelessly, they send you chasing a modal that was working fine.

How Pulzivo detects them

Rage clicks and dead clicks are Enterprise features. They are not on Free, Starter, or Pro. The optional extras script, which also carries form tracking, loads only when the plan enables those modules. The core script stays the smaller file (about 9KB gzip) on plans that do not need them. The grid is on the pricing page.

Rage click: three clicks in one second

The extras script counts a rage click when the same element receives three clicks within one second. "Same element" is the tag name plus its id plus its class list, so two identical buttons with no id can be grouped together, and a button with an id stays distinct. When the threshold is hit, Pulzivo records a rage_click event with the element, the visible text, the page, and the click count, then resets the counter so one frustrated burst does not become a stream of duplicate events.

That definition is narrower than "the visitor seemed annoyed." Three deliberate clicks on a toolbar icon, spaced a second apart, do not qualify. Three clicks in a single second on a button that did not respond do. The docs section that introduces the event is Rage clicks and Web Vitals.

Dead click: nothing visible changed

On each click, the script notes the URL and the scroll position, then checks again 500 milliseconds later. If the URL is the same, the scroll position is the same, and the target is not an input, textarea, select, or label, it records a dead_click with the element, its text, the page, and the href if it had one. Form fields are excluded because focusing a field does not change the URL or the scroll position, and that click was not dead.

This check has a known blind spot. A control that opens a modal, toggles a menu, or updates a panel in place, without changing the URL and without moving the scroll position, can look dead. Treat a dead click as a lead. Confirm it by using the control yourself. If the modal opened, the detector was wrong about that element, and you can ignore that row.

How to work a list of them

Sort by count, not by how dramatic the label sounds. A control with dozens of rage clicks on one page is a broken or slow button. A single dead click on a footer link is noise. For each row you keep, write down the page, the element text, and what you expected to happen.

  • The control does nothing. The handler is missing, the button is disabled without an explanation, or a overlay is intercepting the click. Fix the handler or remove the control.
  • The control is slow. The work ran, but not within a second, so the visitor clicked again. Show a pending state on the first click and ignore further clicks until it finishes. Pair this with Interaction to Next Paint if the whole page feels stuck. That metric is on every plan, including Free, and is covered in Core Web Vitals for site owners.
  • The control looks clickable and is not. A card, a heading, or an icon styled like a button will collect dead clicks from people who believed it was a link. Either make it a link or restyle it so it does not invite a click.
  • The click worked and the detector could not see it. In-page UI, as above. Do not "fix" a working menu because a heuristic flagged it.

Give elements a stable id

The grouping key uses the id when there is one. A button with id="checkout" shows up as its own row. A set of anonymous <div class="card"> elements collapse together, and you cannot tell which card was the problem. Add ids to the controls you care about. You do not need an id on every span.

What to do with the event

Open the events list and filter to rage_click or dead_click. The text and the page are usually enough to reproduce the issue without a recording. Fix the worst page first, deploy, and see whether that row's count drops. A count that stays high after a fix means the fix missed the element people are actually hitting, often a different button with similar text.

Do not page the whole team for these events. They are a weekly review, next to 404s and the slowest Web Vitals. If you are on a plan below Enterprise, you will not have these two events. Scroll depth, click tracking, and Web Vitals are on the free plan and will still show you a page people do not scroll and a page that is slow. Rage and dead clicks are the extra signal when the plan includes them.

If you already know a control is misbehaving, you do not need to wait for a quota. Reproduce it, fix it, and use the events afterward to see whether the burst stopped. When you want them recorded, Enterprise is the plan that includes them. Start free if you still need the base script in place. The extras file is fetched only after the plan turns the module on.
measure-form-abandonment:
Form abandonment is a form someone started and did not submit before they left the page. It is a narrower idea than "they did not convert." A visitor who never focused a field did not abandon the form. They ignored it. The number worth acting on is the gap between people who started and people who submitted, plus which fields they actually touched.

What Pulzivo records

Form tracking is an Enterprise feature, in the same optional extras script as rage clicks and dead clicks. It is not on Free, Starter, or Pro. The core script does not include it. See the pricing page for the plan that does.

The four events

  • form_start fires the first time a visitor focuses an input, textarea, or select in that form. The payload has the form id and the page.
  • form_field_interaction fires on each focus. The field name is the element's name, or its id if there is no name, or the input type if it has neither. This is the event that tells you which fields were touched.
  • form_submit fires on the form's submit event, with how long it had been since the start and the list of field names that were focused.
  • form_abandon fires when the page is unloading, and only if the form was started and at least one field was focused and the form was not submitted. It includes the form id, the page, how many distinct fields were focused, and how long the visitor spent.

Read that last event carefully. fieldsCompleted is the number of distinct fields the visitor focused. The event's totalFields is that same count. The script does not walk the form and count every input that exists. It cannot tell you "they stopped at field 4 of 9" unless you look at the focus events and you know how the form is built. The focus events carry the field names. The abandon event tells you the form was left unfinished.

Name the form and the fields

If the form has no id and no name, every such form on the site is recorded as unknown-form and you cannot tell the signup form from the contact form. Set id or name on the <form>, and set name on each field you want to recognise. name="email" is readable in the event list. A generated id is not. The install for the base script is in the documentation. The extras file is loaded by that script only when the plan includes form tracking.

A weekly review that stays short

Pull two numbers per form: starts, and submits. Abandonment for the week is starts minus submits, for forms that were actually focused. Then open the field-focus events for the form with the worst gap and see which names appear often on abandoned visits and rarely on submitted ones. That field is the one to look at first. Common causes:

  • The field asks for something the visitor does not have ready (a company size, a phone number, a VAT id) with no explanation of why.
  • Validation runs late. The visitor fills five fields, hits submit, and the first field errors in a way that looks like the form ate their work.
  • The form is longer than the decision. A newsletter form with six fields will lose people who would have given an email.
  • The submit control does not look like it worked, so they leave. That can also show up as a rage click on the button. Rage clicks are Enterprise as well, and the way they are counted is in Rage clicks and dead clicks.

Fixes that match the evidence

If almost nobody focuses the form, the problem is the page, not the fields. Move the form, or cut the paragraph above it. If they focus the first field and leave, the first field is the problem. If they focus every field and still do not submit, look at the button, the error text, and anything the submit handler does before the request returns. Do not add a motivational headline. Remove a field, name the error, and keep the values in place when validation fails.

Do not put an email address or a name into a custom event property to "understand" who left. The field-focus event already has the field name, which is what you need. Sending the value turns an anonymous product metric into personal data you did not have to collect. Pulzivo collects no personal data by default. Keep it that way unless you have a separate, deliberate reason and a place to document it.

What you can learn without Enterprise

On the free plan you still have page views, clicks, and custom events. A single signup_completed event, which you send yourself on a successful response, tells you how many people finished. It does not tell you who started and stopped, and it does not name the field. That is the gap form tracking fills, and it is why the feature sits on Enterprise rather than on the free script. If you only have one form and a handful of visits, watch a few people use it, or use it yourself with the network panel open. You do not need a metric to delete two unnecessary fields.

When the form is busy enough that you cannot watch it, the events above are the record. Start free to get the base script on the site. Turn on form tracking when you are on Enterprise and the form id is in place, then read starts against submits before you redesign the whole page.
bounce-rate-without-ga4:
Bounce rate is the share of sessions that ended without a second page view. It is a blunt number. A docs article that answered the question, a blog post that was read to the end, and a broken landing page can all "bounce." GA4 moved its default language toward engagement rate, and the two percentages are not mirrors of each other. If you are reading Pulzivo instead of GA4, you need the definition Pulzivo actually uses, and a better set of questions than "is the rate high?"

The definition in Pulzivo

A session counts as bounced when it has one page view. The bounce rate is that count divided by the number of sessions in the range. Sessions, and the bounce rate that comes from them, are on Starter and above ("session and bounce rate analytics" on the pricing page). They are not on the free plan. The free plan still has page views, clicks, scroll depth, and Core Web Vitals, which are often the more honest signals. More on those below.

This is not Google's engaged-session definition. Google documents an engaged session as one that lasts longer than 10 seconds, or includes a key event, or has two or more page views. A ten-second visit with one page view can be "engaged" in GA4 and "bounced" in Pulzivo. If you are comparing a GA4 engagement rate to a Pulzivo bounce rate, you are comparing two different questions. Do not expect them to add up to 100 percent. The practical difference between the products is on the GA4 alternative page.

Why a high bounce rate is sometimes the goal

A recipe, a changelog, a support answer, and a blog post are often successful when the visitor reads one URL and leaves. They came for that page. A second page view would mean they did not find it. On those URLs, a high bounce rate plus a deep scroll is a good outcome. A high bounce rate plus a few percent of scroll is a page that failed in the first screen.

The opposite is a signup flow or a pricing page. There you want another step: the account form, the docs, the checkout. A high bounce rate on those URLs is a reason to look at the first screen, the load time, and the next link, not a reason to panic about the sitewide average.

What to read instead of one sitewide rate

Split the question by page type before you look at any percentage.

  • Did they stay on the page? Scroll depth is on the free plan and is reported with the page exit. A pricing page whose typical scroll is under a quarter of the document is a first-screen problem. A docs page with a deep scroll and one page view is probably fine.
  • Did the page feel broken? LCP, INP, and CLS are on the free plan. A bounced visit on a page with a poor LCP is a speed problem wearing a bounce costume. The cutoffs and the way to read the 75th percentile are in Core Web Vitals for site owners.
  • Did they do the thing? Send one custom event for the action that matters, such as signup_completed or docs_copied. Custom events are on every plan, including Free. A page with a high bounce rate and a steady stream of that event is doing its job.
  • Did they come from somewhere that promised something else? A campaign that lands on the wrong URL will bounce. UTM attribution, which tells you the campaign, is on Starter, the same plan as the bounce rate. Fix the landing URL before you rewrite the page.

How to use the bounce rate once you have it

On Starter, read bounce rate per entry page, not as one number for the whole property. Sort entry pages by sessions, then look at bounce rate only for pages with enough sessions that a couple of visits cannot swing it. Compare a page to its own previous period. A jump after a deploy is actionable. A stable 70 percent on a blog you have not touched is probably the shape of that content.

Ignore the sitewide rate in a status meeting. It mixes the docs (fine to leave) with the signup page (not fine to leave) and produces a number nobody can act on. If someone asks for it, give them the entry pages instead.

A short routine

Once a week, open the three entry pages that matter: the homepage or the campaign landing page, the pricing page, and the one article or docs URL you are currently sending people to. For each, note sessions if you are on Starter, scroll depth, and whether the custom event fired. If the landing page is slow, check LCP before you touch the copy. If scroll is deep and the event never fires, the ending of the page is the problem, not the headline. If bounce is high and scroll is deep on a blog post, leave it alone.

Pulzivo's session is not a cross-device identity. The default visitor id rotates each calendar day, and a session ends after inactivity. A person who reads an article, leaves, and comes back tomorrow is a new session, and the first of those can be a bounce even though they returned. That is another reason not to treat the rate as a verdict on the content.

Where this leaves the free plan

You can learn a lot before you have a bounce rate. Page views tell you which URLs are used. Scroll depth tells you whether those visits got past the hero. A custom event tells you whether the action happened. Web Vitals tell you whether the page was slow or jumpy. The bounce rate, when you move to Starter, adds the "one page and done" cut on top of that. It does not replace it.

The free plan is 10,000 events a month, one site, no card. Start free, put the script on the pages you are judging, and read scroll and the one custom event for a week before you adopt a bounce target you found on someone else's blog.
add-analytics-to-wordpress-without-googl:
A WordPress site for a shop, a freelance practice, or a personal blog does not need a Google Analytics property before you can see whether anyone opened the homepage. You need the script on every page, and one page view in the dashboard that matches a page you just opened. This is that install. It is not a comparison of analytics products, and it does not ask you to create a Google tag.

What you are adding

Pulzivo is one script tag. The file is about 9KB gzipped. You paste it into the header so WordPress prints it on each public page. Page views are recorded on their own. The free plan is 10,000 events a month, one website, and 30 days of retention. It includes page view tracking, click tracking, custom event tracking, scroll depth, and Web Vitals. It does not include the visitor count, sessions, or campaign reports. Those start on Starter. The grid is on the pricing page.

Pulzivo sets no cookies and collects no personal data by default. That describes the script. It is not a promise about banners or about other plugins you already run. A contact form, an embedded map, and a font can still store their own data. The longer checklist for that is in privacy-friendly analytics for small sites.

There is no Pulzivo plugin in the WordPress directory. Do not install a random "analytics" plugin and hope it is this one. You either paste the tag with a header plugin, or you paste it into the theme header. Both end at the same tag.

Get the key and the tag

Create an account, open Dashboard, then API Keys, and copy the key that starts with PULZ-. The tag, with your key in place of the placeholder, is:

<script src="https://cdn.pulzivo.com/pulzivo-analytics.min.js"
        data-api-key="YOUR_API_KEY"></script>

Leave the address as it is. A typo in the file name loads nothing, and the dashboard stays empty for a reason that looks like "no traffic." The same tag is in the documentation, including the WordPress steps this page follows.

The header plugin, which is the easier path

In the WordPress dashboard go to Plugins, then Add New, and search for Insert Headers and Footers. The plugin is often listed under the name WPCode. Install it and activate it. Open its header box. In the docs that box is Settings, then Insert Headers and Footers. If the menu uses the WPCode name, open that menu and use the header field. Paste the tag into the box for scripts in the header. Save.

Use the header box, not the footer box. The script is meant to load with the page. A footer paste can still work, but a header paste matches the way the product is documented, and it runs before a visitor hits the back button on a short visit.

If Plugins, then Add New, is missing, the host is not letting you add plugins. That is common on a free WordPress.com site. The theme-file path below has the same limit when the host hides the theme editor. In that case the plan on the host, not Pulzivo, is what you have to change before a script can be added.

The theme file, if you would rather not add a plugin

Go to Appearance, then Theme File Editor, and open header.php. Paste the tag just before </head>. Update the file. A child theme is the safer place to do this. If you edit the parent theme, the next theme update can replace header.php and silently remove the tag. You would notice only because new visits stopped.

Do this on a staging copy if you have one. If you only have the live site, copy the file's contents somewhere before you change them, so you can put the old header back. You are editing a file WordPress uses on every page. A broken header is a broken site, which is why the plugin path is the one to prefer when you are not comfortable in that editor.

Confirm that a page view arrived

Open the public site in a browser, not the WordPress customizer preview. Click the homepage, or any page a customer would open. The script sends events about every 5 seconds, and it also sends them when you leave the tab. Switch to the Pulzivo dashboard. A new site shows "Waiting for your first visit" until something arrives. Give it a few seconds and refresh the overview if the row is not there yet.

You are looking for a page view of the path you opened, such as / or /contact. The Events list shows the same visit if you want the raw row. One page view is enough to prove the tag ran. You do not need a day of traffic before you trust the install.

If nothing appears, check four things in this order. View the page source on the public URL and search for pulzivo-analytics.min.js. If it is missing, the plugin did not save, or a cache is still serving the old HTML. Clear the cache in your caching plugin, or in the host's cache, and reload. If the tag is in the source but the key is still YOUR_API_KEY, paste the real key. If the tag and the key are right, open the site in a private window. A browser you already marked to ignore your own visits will not send the page view, and the install can look broken when it is not.

A page builder that loads a different header on the homepage is a separate trap. Check the source on the homepage and on one inner page. Both should contain the tag. If only one does, the header plugin is not actually site-wide, and the theme is injecting a second header. Put the tag in the header that both templates use.

What you can read on the free plan

After the first page view, the free plan will keep counting page views, clicks on elements you mark, custom events you send, scroll depth, and Web Vitals. The Visitors number and the Sessions number stay locked until Starter. That is the pricing page, not a bug in the WordPress install. A quiet brochure site often stays inside 10,000 events a month. Each page view counts as an event, and so does a click or a custom event, so a site with a lot of clicks uses the allowance faster than a site people only read.

You can leave Google Analytics in place while you do this. The two scripts do not have to match each other's totals. Ad blockers, caches, and different definitions move the numbers. Use Pulzivo for the questions on the pricing page, and decide later whether you still open the Google property. A fair version of that choice is in a simple Google Analytics alternative.

Put it on the live header and check one page

Install the header plugin or edit the child theme, paste the tag, clear the cache, and open the public homepage once. When that page view is in the dashboard, the install is done. Start free. The free plan does not ask for a card.
add-analytics-to-shopify-without-ga4:
A small Shopify store does not have to connect Google Analytics 4 before you can see product-page traffic. Pulzivo does not have an app in the Shopify App Store, and this guide will not send you looking for one. You paste a script into the theme, the same way the product documentation describes it, and then you confirm that one product page showed up as a page view.

What this paste does and does not cover

The file you edit, layout/theme.liquid, is the frame around the online store: the homepage, collections, products, pages, and the blog, as long as they use that theme. Checkout is a different Shopify page. Pasting into the theme does not add the script to checkout, and Pulzivo does not ship a checkout extension to do it for you. If you need purchase totals, you will not get them from this step. You will get the storefront: which products were opened, which collection sent people onward, and whether the homepage is the page they actually see.

The free plan records those page views. It is 10,000 events a month, one website, and 30 days of retention, with click tracking, custom events, scroll depth, and Web Vitals included. Sessions, unique visitors, and UTM attribution are on Starter, not on Free. Read the line items on the pricing page before you assume a report is missing because the theme paste failed.

Pulzivo sets no cookies and collects no personal data by default. Shopify, your payment apps, and any other script in the theme can still set their own. Adding this tag does not remove theirs.

Paste the tag into the theme

Copy your API key from Dashboard, then API Keys. It starts with PULZ-. The tag is the same one used on any other site:

<script src="https://cdn.pulzivo.com/pulzivo-analytics.min.js"
        data-api-key="YOUR_API_KEY"></script>

In Shopify admin, open Online Store, then Themes. On the current theme, open Edit code. The menu is sometimes labeled Actions, and sometimes it is the three dots. Open layout/theme.liquid. Search for the closing </head> tag and paste the script on the line just before it. Save.

That is the path in the documentation. There is no second, app-based path. If a search in the App Store returns other analytics apps, those are different products.

Duplicate the theme if you want a way back

You are editing a live theme when you follow the steps above on the published theme. If you want a backup first, duplicate the theme, edit the copy, preview it, and publish that copy when the page view shows up. Shopify keeps the previous theme in the library, so you can publish it again if a liquid error takes the storefront down. A missing </head> or a paste in the middle of another tag is the usual cause. Put the script on its own lines, immediately above the closing head tag, and do not wrap it in liquid unless you already know you need a conditional.

Online Store 2.0 themes still use theme.liquid for the head. You do not add the script as a section on the homepage. A section would track only the pages where you placed that section. The layout file tracks every page that uses the theme.

One theme means one paste

If you publish a different theme later, for a season or a redesign, the new theme has its own theme.liquid. The script does not move with the products. After you publish the new theme, open its layout file and paste the tag again, then repeat the check below. A store that "used to track and then stopped" after a theme swap is usually this.

Confirm a product page, not the admin

Open the storefront in a normal browser window. Use the public URL, not the Shopify admin and not the theme editor's preview pane. Open one product page a customer can reach. The script sends a batch about every 5 seconds, and it sends again when you leave the tab. Switch to the Pulzivo dashboard. A new key shows a waiting state until the first event arrives. Refresh the overview after a few seconds.

Look for a page view whose path is that product, often something like /products/your-product. If you only see the homepage, you confirmed the wrong URL. If you see nothing, view the source of the product page and search for pulzivo-analytics.min.js. Missing tag means the paste was saved on a theme that is not the published one. A tag with YOUR_API_KEY still in it means the placeholder was not replaced. A correct tag and no event means this browser may already be set to skip your visits. Retry in a private window, where that setting does not exist.

Shopify's own analytics will not match these numbers, and they do not need to. You are checking that Pulzivo saw the page, not that two dashboards print the same integer.

What to do after the first product view

Leave the tag in place and use the store for a normal day before you judge volume. A product view, a collection view, and the homepage are three page views and three events. Clicks count as well when they are recorded. A busy catalog can use 10,000 events a month faster than a three-page brochure. The free plan is the right place to learn that, because it does not ask for a card. Move up only when the allowance or a locked report, such as sessions, is the thing you actually need.

If the shop also has a WordPress blog on another domain, that is a second website. The free plan includes one website. The WordPress install is a separate paste, described in how to add analytics to WordPress without Google. Do not point both sites at one key and expect the pricing page's "1 website" line to stretch.

Campaign links, such as the URL you put in an email or on a social profile, are a later step. The theme paste does not invent them. Get the product page view first.

Save the theme and open one product

Edit code on the theme customers see, paste the script above </head>, save, and open one product on the public store. When that path is a page view, the storefront is instrumented. Checkout remains out of scope on purpose. Start free if you still need the key.
analytics-script-on-wix-squarespace-webf:
Wix, Squarespace, and Webflow all hide the header behind a settings screen. None of them needs a developer if the plan on that host lets you paste custom code. The Pulzivo piece is the same script tag on all three. The clicks to reach the header are not. This page is those three paths, plus the check that tells you the paste is live.

The tag, once

Copy the API key from Dashboard, then API Keys. It starts with PULZ-. Paste this, with your key, into the header field on the host. Do not add <html> or <body> around it. Those hosts inject the snippet into a page that already has a head.

<script src="https://cdn.pulzivo.com/pulzivo-analytics.min.js"
        data-api-key="YOUR_API_KEY"></script>

The free plan is 10,000 events a month, one website, and 30 days of retention. Page views, click tracking, custom events, scroll depth, and Web Vitals are included. Visitors, sessions, and UTM attribution are not. That split is on the pricing page. Pulzivo sets no cookies and collects no personal data by default. The host's own scripts are separate.

The same tag and the Webflow steps are in the documentation. Wix and Squarespace are not given their own tabs there, so the click paths below follow each host's current help, not a Pulzivo app. There is no Pulzivo app to install on these three.

Wix

Wix's own help (Embedding Custom Code, updated in 2026) says to start with a published site that has a connected domain. In the site dashboard, open Settings, then Custom Code, under Development and integrations. Some accounts still show Custom Code under Advanced. Choose Add Custom Code, paste the tag, and name it something you will recognize, such as Pulzivo.

Under Add Code to Pages, choose All pages, and load the code on each page a visitor opens. "Once per visit" skips later pages in that visit, so the dashboard would under-count page views. Under Place Code in, choose Head. Apply.

Custom code runs on the published site, not inside the editor. Open the live domain when you check. Wix also says that Google Analytics, Google Tag Manager, and the Facebook and TikTok pixels do not run through this custom-code box, and that those belong in Wix's marketing integrations. Pulzivo is not one of those named tools. Still, the proof is a page view, not the Apply button. If the live page source has no pulzivo-analytics.min.js, Wix did not emit the snippet, and that is a Wix limit to take up with their help rather than a missing Pulzivo setting.

Squarespace

Squarespace's help says code injection is on the Core, Plus, and Advanced plans, and on some older plans. Checkout pages do not support it. On a 7.1 site, open the Pages panel, go to Custom Code at the bottom, and open Code Injection. On a 7.0 site the same panel is under Website Tools, then Code Injection. Paste the tag into the Header field, not the Footer field, and save.

The Header field is added to the head of every page. A single-page header, under page settings and Advanced, only covers that page, so a blog would be missed. Use the site-wide Header field unless you have a reason to track one URL. The Squarespace app on a phone does not offer this panel. Use a computer.

If you cannot find the field, the plan is the usual reason. Squarespace's help page for code injection is the list to check, because plan names move and this article should not invent a price for them.

Webflow

Webflow's help calls the screen Site settings, then the Custom code tab, then Head code. Older screens say Project settings, which is the name in Pulzivo's docs. Paste the tag into Head code, save, and publish the site. Webflow is explicit that custom code can show in preview and still stay off the live site until you publish. Skip that publish and the check below will fail on the real domain.

Webflow's help says site managers and designers can add this when the workspace is on Core, Growth, Agency, or Freelancer, or when the site itself has an active site plan. If the Head code box is missing or locked, that requirement is what to check. A site plan on a different Webflow project does not unlock this one. Do not paste a full HTML document into the box. The script tag is the whole snippet.

Confirm the live page, then stop

Open the published URL in a normal browser. Do not stop at the editor canvas. Click the homepage. The script sends about every 5 seconds, and again when you leave the tab. Open the Pulzivo dashboard. A new site says it is waiting for the first visit until an event arrives. Refresh after a few seconds and look for a page view of /.

Then open one inner page, such as the contact page or a service page, and look for that path too. A header paste that only landed on the homepage is a per-page code block, not the site-wide field. View source on both URLs and search for the script file name. Both should contain it, and the key should be yours, not YOUR_API_KEY.

A private window is the clean retest if you have already told Pulzivo to ignore that browser. The editor's preview is not a substitute. Hosts differ on whether preview runs custom code, and a preview-only success does not mean a visitor on the real domain is counted.

These builders also cache. After you change the header, publish again, or republish the site, before you decide the tag is wrong. An old published version is the most common "I pasted it and nothing happened" on Webflow and Squarespace.

Three hosts, one thing to prove

Wix needs Head, all pages, each page load, on the published domain. Squarespace needs the site-wide Header field in code injection, on a plan that includes it. Webflow needs Head code saved and the site published. The store equivalent, if you also sell on Shopify, is a theme file rather than a settings box, and it is written up in how to add analytics to Shopify without GA4. Do not look for a Pulzivo listing in any of these app markets.

When both the homepage and one inner page show as page views, you are done. Start free to get the key. No card is required on the free plan.
which-social-or-google-visit-reached-you:
A tap on your Facebook page, your Instagram bio, or the website button on your Google Business profile only matters if that person landed on the site. The app often hides where they came from. This page is how to tell a real arrival from a guess, in plain language. The rules for naming campaign links live in a separate article. This one is the problem those links solve.

Two different clues

A referrer is the previous page, when the browser is willing to say so. Open a link on a normal website, and the next site can often see the domain you left. Open the same link inside the Facebook or Instagram app, and the browser inside that app frequently sends nothing. The visit still happened. The "where from" line is blank, and the dashboard files it as direct: someone who looks like they typed the address or used a bookmark.

Pulzivo names the referrer when it is present. A host under facebook.com, plus fb.com and fb.me, is shown as Facebook. instagram.com is shown as Instagram. A google domain is shown as Google. Those names are labels for the domain that was sent. They are not a list of people, and they are not a claim that every social tap will carry the domain. If the app sends no referrer, there is nothing to rename. The row is direct.

Google is the awkward case. A search result and the website button on your Business profile can both arrive as Google, or the Business profile tap can arrive as direct because the app dropped the referrer. Two visits that both say Google are not "one from search and one from the listing." You cannot split them after the fact.

What the dashboard will show, and on which plan

Top sources and campaign names are the UTM and attribution reports. The pricing page lists UTM and attribution tracking on Starter, not on Free. On the free plan the page view is still recorded, so you can see that the URL was opened. You cannot see the source breakdown until the plan includes it. Upgrading does not invent a source. A visit that arrived with no referrer and no campaign label stays direct.

The free plan remains 10,000 events a month, one website, and 30 days of retention, with page views included. Starter is the plan that adds the source list, along with sessions and unique visitors. The lines are on the pricing page.

A campaign link is a label you stick on the URL

When you control the link, you can add a short query that says which button it was. The visitor lands on the same page. The extra words ride along in the address. Pulzivo reads them on that first page, which is what you want, because some site builders rewrite the address a moment later and would otherwise throw the label away.

You do not need a different website for Facebook, Instagram, and the Business profile. You need the same page three times, each with its own label. One set, for a bakery site, looks like this:

https://example.com/?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=bio
https://example.com/?utm_source=instagram&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=bio
https://example.com/?utm_source=google&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=business-profile

Put the Facebook line in the Facebook website field or the post, the Instagram line in the bio, and the Google line in the Business profile website button. Use lowercase, and use the same campaign word for as long as you want those taps added together. A source that says Google is grouped with search. The campaign name business-profile is the label that separates the listing from an ordinary Google visit, so read the campaign, not only the word Google. The spelling rules, which medium names get grouped, and why you must not add these parameters to links inside your own site, are already written in how to track UTM campaigns. Follow that page rather than inventing a second style here. Build the address in the UTM campaign URL builder so a missing piece does not ship. The builder stays in the browser and does not upload the URL.

Why a bare "website" button fails the question

The button on a Facebook page, the link in an Instagram bio, and the website field on a Business profile all accept a normal URL. If you paste https://example.com with nothing after it, you are back to the referrer. Sometimes Facebook shows up. Often it does not. Google may show up and be indistinguishable from search. The campaign link is the version that still answers "which button" when the referrer is missing or is only the word Google.

Write the three addresses down next to where you pasted them. Six months from now the bio is the place you will forget. If you change the campaign word, you start a new row. That is useful when the offer changed, and noisy when you only wanted a running total.

Check one tap before you announce it

Paste one of the three links into a post or the profile, then open it yourself on a phone, because that is how your customers open it. Land on the site. On Starter, the source list should gain a row for that source and campaign after the page view is in. On Free, confirm the page view of the path you used, and expect the campaign row to appear once the plan includes attribution. Do not judge the link from a desktop preview of the social app if you can open the real app. The in-app browser is the one that drops referrers.

If the row says direct and the address bar still shows utm_source when the page loads, the parameters arrived and the report plan is the gap. If the address bar never shows them, the social app or the profile field stripped the query. Some fields only accept a "clean" URL. When that happens, a short link you control, which redirects to the tagged address, is the workaround. Pulzivo does not provide that shortener. Any redirect you already trust is enough, as long as the browser ends on your domain with the parameters still there.

Give the button a week before you rank the channels. A single test tap from you is a check that the label works. It is not a measure of the audience. And if this browser is set to ignore your own visits, your test tap will not appear at all. Use a private window for the check.

What a label will not tell you

It will not name the person. It will not survive if they copy the address and delete the question mark before they send it to a friend. It will not repair last month's posts, which already went out with a bare URL. It will not, by itself, tell you that they called or bought. A page view with a campaign label means they reached the site from that button. A later action is a separate event.

Keep the three links stable, send people to a page that matches the promise in the post, and read sources on Starter when you need the split. The free plan can still hold the page views while you decide. Start free if the script is not on the site yet. The tag has to be there before any label can be recorded.
track-phone-and-email-clicks:
On a small business site, the phone number and the email address are often the real conversion. A page view of the contact page does not tell you that anyone tapped Call or Email. Those taps are easy to miss, because a tel: link and a mailto: link are not ordinary web links. This is how to count them, and which plan actually includes the feature you are about to use.

What is counted without any extra markup

Pulzivo records an outbound click when someone follows a link to another website, meaning an address that starts with http or https. A phone link starts with tel:. An email link starts with mailto:. The outbound check skips both. A tap that opens the phone dialer, or the mail app, does not show up as an outbound click. If you have been looking for those taps in a list of other websites, they were never going to be there.

File downloads are the other automatic case, and they are also not this. A PDF of a menu is a download. A tap on the phone number in the footer is not.

Free plan: mark the link, or send a named event

The pricing page includes click tracking and custom event tracking on the Free plan. Two different tools sit under those lines.

Click tracking on every plan records an element you mark with data-click. On the phone link and the email link, that looks like this:

<a href="tel:+14165550199" data-click="phone">Call</a>
<a href="mailto:hello@example.com" data-click="email">Email</a>

The event name is click. The data-click value is stored with it, so you can tell a phone tap from an email tap in the event list. You do not send the visitor's number or their email. The business number in the link is the number you already show the public. Leave the visitor's details out of the event.

A goal is a name you add in the dashboard. The documentation says goals are available on every plan, including Free. The pricing page does not list "goals" as its own row. It lists custom event tracking on Free, and that is the feature a named event uses. A goal matches an event whose name is the word you typed, or a goal sent with the goal call. It does not match the data-click label. A goal called phone stays at zero if the only event you produced is a click with that label. The event name and the label are different fields.

When you want a goal, send a custom event whose name is the goal. On a site where you can edit the link HTML, a phone link can do both jobs:

<a href="tel:+14165550199"
   onclick="if (window.PulzivoAnalytics) PulzivoAnalytics('event', 'phone_click')">Call</a>

Use email_click on the mailto link. In the dashboard, open Goals and add an event goal with that exact name. The count is visitors who viewed a page and also fired the event. Someone who fired the event with no page view is not a conversion. The free allowance is still 10,000 events a month. Each custom event counts toward it, the same way a page view does.

Starter: automatic clicks on the link itself

The pricing page lists auto click and scroll tracking on Starter, and the comparison table marks auto click tracking off for Free. On Starter and above, a click on a link or a button is recorded even without data-click. That includes a tel: link and a mailto: link. The event is still named click, and the address is on the event, so you can see the phone number or the mailbox that was tapped.

That is the path when the site builder will not let you edit the link HTML. Wix, Squarespace, and a lot of themes give you a URL field and no attribute field. You put tel: or mailto: in the URL, and Starter's auto click is what records the tap. A named goal still needs the custom event above, because a goal does not read the link address. If you cannot add the onclick, read the click list and the address on each row, and do not expect a goal called phone_click to fill itself in.

Auto click will also record other links and buttons. The phone row is the one whose address starts with tel:. It is not a separate report with that title.

Where you can actually edit the link

In WordPress, open the paragraph or the button, choose edit as HTML, and add the attribute or the onclick to the anchor. The header script from the install has to be on the page already, or PulzivoAnalytics does not exist and the onclick does nothing. The install itself is how to add analytics to WordPress without Google.

On Wix, Squarespace, or Webflow, a header paste does not by itself mark the phone link. If the builder lets you add HTML on that one button, use the snippet above. If it only lets you set the link URL, use a tel: URL and read auto clicks on Starter. The header steps for those three hosts are in how to add the script on Wix, Squarespace, or Webflow. Do not put the visitor's email address in the event to "see who clicked." The field name is enough, and the product collects no personal data unless you choose to send some.

A check that takes one tap

Publish the page. On your phone, tap Call, then cancel the dialer so you do not ring yourself. Tap Email, then close the draft. Wait a few seconds. The script sends about every 5 seconds and also when the tab is hidden. In the dashboard, open Events and look for phone_click or email_click if you used the custom event, or for a click whose address is the tel: or mailto: link if you are on Starter's auto clicks.

Then add the goal only after you have seen the event name once. A goal created for a name that never fires looks like a broken contact page. It is usually a mismatched name. phone_click and phone-click are not the same goal.

The documentation shows the event call and the goal call if you would rather use PulzivoAnalytics('goal', 'phone_click'). That stores an event named goal with the label phone_click, and the goals screen matches the label. Either the custom event or the goal call works on the free plan. Pick one and use it on both the header and the footer, or you will split one phone number into two names.

Repeat the tap in a private window if your everyday browser is excluded from tracking. An excluded browser sends nothing, so the test looks like the attribute was ignored.

Count the tap, not the page

A contact page can be busy while the phone link stays idle, or the other way around. Mark the link, or rely on Starter's auto click when you cannot mark it, and read the event before you rewrite the page. Custom events are on the free plan. The goal screen is documented for every plan, including Free, and it is not a separate line on the pricing page. Start free, put the script on the site, and tap the number once from a phone before you treat a week of contact-page views as demand.
exclude-your-own-visits:
On a quiet site, the most active visitor is often you. You check the homepage after a text change, you open the contact page on your phone, and the dashboard looks like a good morning. Owner mode is how Pulzivo leaves those visits out. It is a flag in the browser you use, not a filter on your customers.

The flag the script actually reads

Open any page of your own site with ?pulz_owner=1 on the end of the address. The script sees that parameter and writes pulz_is_owner in that browser's localStorage, with the value true. The next page loads read the same key. You can close the tab. The flag stays until you clear it or you clear the site's stored data.

A full address looks like https://example.com/?pulz_owner=1. If the page already has a question mark, add the piece with an ampersand instead: https://example.com/contact?ref=1&pulz_owner=1. Two other names do the same job, exclude_owner and pulz_exclude_owner. You only need one. ?pulz_owner=1 is the one to remember.

Any value other than a deliberate off turns the flag on. ?pulz_owner=1 is the clear choice. To turn it off, open a page with ?pulz_owner=0. The values false, no, and off also turn it off. Off removes pulz_is_owner from localStorage. It does not write the word false and leave a key behind.

What gets dropped

While the flag is on, that browser sends nothing. Page views, clicks, custom events, scroll, and Web Vitals are all suppressed. There is no error on the page. The site works. The dashboard simply does not gain a row for what you just did. The suppression starts when the flag is applied, including events that were waiting to be sent.

This is per browser, on the site's own domain. Turning it on in Chrome on your laptop does not turn it on in Safari, in a private window, or on your phone. Each of those has its own localStorage. If you edit the site from three places, set the flag in each one you want ignored. A private window is useful for the opposite reason: it does not have the flag, so it is how you confirm that a normal visitor is still counted.

Do not put ?pulz_owner=1 in a link you give to a customer, a newsletter, or an ad. Whoever opens that link sets the flag in their browser, and their later visits on that browser disappear too. The parameter is for you, once, on your own devices.

The same switch in the dashboard

Dashboard, then Settings, then Analytics, has "Exclude my visits on this browser." Turning that on opens your site in a new tab with ?pulz_owner=1. It does not write the flag inside the dashboard's own storage and hope the shop site notices. The shop site is a different address, and only the shop site can store the key visitors' browsers would use. The settings button is a convenient way to open the right URL. The URL is what the script reads. The documentation lists this as the no-console method, next to the other ways a developer might set the same key.

There is a second control in that settings section: exclude visits when you are signed in as your account email, plus a list of other emails. That one runs on the server, and it only matches an event that actually carries that email or user id. On a normal small-business site, Pulzivo does not collect an email by default, and a stable id is only sent if you opt in and supply one, which is a Pro feature. Anonymous browsing by you, the owner, clicking around the public site, does not carry your login email. The email switch will not hide those visits. The browser flag will. Use the flag for the laptop and the phone you test with. Use the email list only if you have deliberately identified signed-in users and you know those events contain the address.

How to tell that it worked

Set the flag, then reload the public homepage in that same browser. Note the page-view total, wait long enough for a send (about 5 seconds, or switch away from the tab, which sends immediately), and refresh the dashboard. The total should not move. Then open a private window, load the same homepage, and refresh the dashboard again. That visit should appear. If the private window also produces nothing, the script is missing or the key is wrong, and the flag is not the problem. The install check in how to add analytics to WordPress without Google is the list to walk, or the equivalent steps for the host you use.

If the normal window still adds page views after ?pulz_owner=1, view the application storage for your domain and look for pulz_is_owner. The value has to be the string true. A blocker that disables storage, or a browser setting that wipes site data when the tab closes, will drop the key and you will be counted again on the next visit. In that browser, set the flag at the start of each editing session, or use a normal window that keeps site data.

What owner mode is not

It is not a privacy setting for your visitors. It does not change what the script collects from everyone else. The default for a visitor is still no cookies and no personal data collected by the analytics script. The visitor id, and the fact that it changes each calendar day, is explained in what cookieless analytics means. Owner mode is a separate key, pulz_is_owner, used only so your own browser stops sending.

It is also not a way to delete history. Visits you already sent stay in the dashboard until retention drops them. The free plan keeps 30 days. Turning the flag on today does not erase yesterday's test clicks. From today forward, that browser stays quiet.

It does not follow you across a new computer. It does not apply to a teammate who uses their own laptop, unless they open the owner link themselves or you add them to the email exclusion and their events actually include that email. For a two-person shop, each person sets the flag on the browsers they use to preview the site.

Set it once on the browsers you edit from

Open the live site with ?pulz_owner=1, confirm a private window still produces a page view, and leave the flag in place on the machines you work from. Your customers never see the parameter. Start free if the script is not installed yet. The flag only matters after the tag is on the page.
page-view-visitor-and-session:
The overview on a small site shows three words that sound like the same idea: page views, visitors, and sessions. They are three counts of one visit, and the free plan does not show all of them. This is the glossary. It is the definitions Pulzivo uses, and the list of what stays on screen when you have not upgraded.

A page view is one look at one address

A page view is recorded when a page loads, and again when the address changes without a full reload, which is how some builders move from the homepage to a contact page. The event name is page_view. Open the homepage, then the menu, then the contact page, and you have three page views if each of those was a new address. Refresh the contact page and you have another one. The path is what you see in the page list, such as / or /contact.

Page view tracking is on the free plan. It is the number you can trust on day one, including the single page view you use to prove the script is installed. The free plan is 10,000 events a month, one website, and 30 days of retention. A page view is an event. So is a click, a custom event, a scroll measurement, and a Web Vital. They share that 10,000. A site that records a lot of clicks uses the month faster than a site that only records page views. The lines are on the pricing page.

A page view is not a person. It is not a sale. It is not proof the page was read. Someone who opens a page and leaves immediately is still a page view. Scroll depth, which is also on the free plan, is the closer hint that they moved down the page. A page view with almost no scroll is a page they did not stay with.

A visitor is one browser, for one calendar day

By default Pulzivo keeps an anonymous id in the browser and stamps it with the calendar day. The same browser, the same day, opening ten pages, is one visitor. The next calendar day, that browser gets a new id. Nothing in the default id ties today to yesterday. A phone and a laptop are two visitors even when the same person is holding both, because they do not share the id. Pulzivo sets no cookies and collects no personal data by default, so it does not try to recognize you across devices.

The Visitors number on the overview is not on the free plan. The pricing page marks unique visitor tracking as a Starter feature, and the overview locks that card until the plan includes it. The id still exists underneath, because page views need a way to be sent, but the distinct-visitor total is a Starter report. Do not refresh the free dashboard looking for a bug when the visitors card is locked. That is the plan.

A stable id, one that lasts past midnight, exists only if you pass an id you already have. That opt-in is on Pro, and it is described on the pricing page as identifying signed-in users with IDs you supply. A brochure site with no accounts should leave it off. You do not need a stable id to know that the contact page was opened. The day-sized id, and what is stored besides it, is covered in what cookieless analytics means. The short version for this glossary: a "visitor" in the default product is a browser-day, not a customer record.

Returning, in this product, is not "came back next week"

Because the default id changes each day, "came back on Thursday" is a new visitor id, not a return attached to Monday. The new-versus-returning split on the overview depends on the session features, which are Starter. Even then, do not read it as a loyalty program. It is the product's own rule for a first session versus a later one, not a name and a face. If you need Monday's reader and Thursday's reader to be the same row, you would have to supply your own id on Pro. Most small sites should not.

A session is one sitting

A session ends after 30 minutes without activity, and it is shared across tabs in that browser. Open the homepage, read the about page, get distracted, and come back 40 minutes later: that is a second session. Open three tabs within the half hour: still one session. The id for it lives in the browser next to the visitor id. It is not a login.

The Sessions number, bounce rate, average time, and pages per visit are on Starter. The pricing page calls this session and bounce rate analytics, and unique visitors are the line above it. On Free those cards are locked. A bounced session, once you have sessions, is a session with one page view. How to read that without panicking, especially on a page that is supposed to answer one question, is in bounce rate without GA4. This glossary only needs the definition: one page view inside the sitting.

One person, walked through the three words

Sam finds your site, opens the homepage, then the contact page, within a few minutes, on one phone, on a Tuesday. That is two page views, one visitor, and one session. Sam calls you from the contact page. The call is not a third page view. It is a tap, and it is only in the dashboard if you tracked the phone link. Sam opens the site again on Wednesday. That is a new visitor id under the default, and a new session, plus whatever pages load on Wednesday.

If you, the owner, did all of that while testing, those counts are you. Owner mode keeps that browser out. The flag is ?pulz_owner=1, stored as pulz_is_owner, and the steps are in how to exclude your own visits. Exclude yourself before you treat a Tuesday with two page views as demand.

What the free plan shows, and what it leaves off

On Free you can read page views, click tracking, custom events, scroll depth, and Web Vitals (LCP, INP, and CLS), for 30 days, on one website, up to 10,000 events a month. You cannot read the visitors total, sessions, bounce rate, entry and exit pages, geography, or UTM and attribution. Those are marked off for Free on the pricing comparison, and on for Starter or a higher plan. Performance metrics, error tracking, and identifying signed-in users are Pro. Form tracking and rage clicks are Enterprise. If a card is locked, the glossary definition still applies. The number is waiting on the plan, not on more traffic.

Use page views to see which addresses were opened. Use scroll depth to see whether those opens got past the first screen. Use one custom event for the action that matters, such as a completed contact form, which is included on Free. Add Starter when you need the visitor count, the session count, or the source of the visit. You do not need Starter to know the site is alive.

Read the unlocked number first

A page view is an address that loaded. A visitor is one browser for that calendar day, and the total is a Starter number. A session is a sitting that expires after 30 quiet minutes, and that total is a Starter number too. On the free plan, start with page views and the one action you care about. Start free. No card is required, and the visitors card can stay locked until you actually need it.
